name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Attachment of proximal end of stamen filament

questiontext.text: In a typical angiosperm flower, the proximal end of the filament of a stamen is attached to which part of the flower?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical stamen consists of two parts: a long, slender stalk called the filament and a terminal bilobed structure called the anther.

Step 2: Application
The distal end of the filament bears the anther, whereas the proximal end of the filament is attached either to the thalamus (receptacle) or to the petal of the flower.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The proximal end of the filament is attached to the thalamus or the petal of the flower.

answer.text: Thalamus or petal
Stigma or style
Ovary wall or placenta
Connective or theca

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Structure of a typical dithecous angiosperm anther

questiontext.text: A typical angiosperm anther is described as bilobed, dithecous, and tetragonal. How many microsporangia are present in such an anther?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical angiosperm anther has two lobes (bilobed), and each lobe has two theca (dithecous).

Step 2: Application
In transverse section, the anther is a four-sided (tetragonal) structure consisting of four microsporangia located at the four corners—two in each lobe.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A typical dithecous angiosperm anther contains four microsporangia (two in each lobe).

answer.text: Two microsporangia, one in each lobe
Four microsporangia, two in each lobe
Eight microsporangia, four in each lobe
One microsporangium shared by both lobes

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Characteristics and function of tapetum

questiontext.text: Which wall layer of the microsporangium possesses cells with dense cytoplasm and generally more than one nucleus to nourish developing pollen grains?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical microsporangium is surrounded by four wall layers: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, and tapetum.

Step 2: Application
The innermost wall layer is the tapetum, which nourishes the developing pollen grains. Its cells possess dense cytoplasm and generally have more than one nucleus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The tapetum is the innermost nutritive wall layer of the microsporangium.

answer.text: Epidermis
Endothecium
Tapetum
Middle layers

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Role of outer three microsporangium wall layers

questiontext.text: In a microsporangium, what are the primary functions performed by the outer three wall layers—epidermis, endothecium, and middle layers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The four wall layers of a microsporangium are functionally divided into the outer three layers and the innermost tapetum.

Step 2: Application
While the innermost tapetum nourishes developing pollen grains, the outer three wall layers (epidermis, endothecium, and middle layers) perform the function of protection and help in the dehiscence of the anther to release the pollen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The outer three wall layers provide protection and assist in anther dehiscence to release pollen.

answer.text: Nutrition of microspores and synthesis of sporopollenin
Meiotic division to form microspore tetrads
Secretion of nectar to attract pollinators
Protection and helping in dehiscence of anther to release pollen

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Ploidy during microsporogenesis

questiontext.text: During microsporogenesis in an angiosperm anther, what are the ploidy levels of a pollen mother cell (PMC) and each cell of the resulting microspore tetrad, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Microsporogenesis is the process of formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell (PMC) through meiosis.

Step 2: Application
Each cell of the diploid sporogenous tissue acts as a potential pollen mother cell (\(2n\)). When the PMC undergoes meiotic division (reduction division), it produces a cluster of four haploid (\(n\)) cells called a microspore tetrad.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pollen mother cell is diploid (\(2n\)) and each cell of the microspore tetrad is haploid (\(n\)).

answer.text: Diploid (\(2n\)) and haploid (\(n\))
Haploid (\(n\)) and haploid (\(n\))
Diploid (\(2n\)) and diploid (\(2n\))
Triploid (\(3n\)) and haploid (\(n\))

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Properties of sporopollenin in pollen exine

questiontext.text: Pollen grains are well-preserved as fossils primarily because their hard outer layer (exine) is composed of which resistant organic material?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pollen grains have a prominent two-layered wall: an outer exine and an inner intine.

Step 2: Application
The hard outer exine is made up of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known. It can withstand high temperatures, strong acids, and alkalis, and no enzyme that degrades sporopollenin is known so far.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sporopollenin in the exine accounts for the exceptional chemical resistance and fossil preservation of pollen grains.

answer.text: Cellulose and pectin
Sporopollenin
Lignin and suberin
Callose

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Intine composition and germ pores

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the inner wall (intine) and germ pores of a typical angiosperm pollen grain?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The pollen grain wall consists of an outer sculptured exine with apertures and an inner continuous intine.

Step 2: Application
The intine is a thin and continuous layer made up of cellulose and pectin. The exine has prominent apertures called germ pores where sporopollenin is absent, allowing the pollen tube to emerge through one of them upon germination.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The intine is a thin, continuous layer of cellulose and pectin, while germ pores are apertures in the exine lacking sporopollenin.

answer.text: The intine is discontinuous and composed of sporopollenin, while germ pores are rich in pectin.
The intine is thick and lignified, while germ pores are regions of extra sporopollenin deposition.
The intine is a thin, continuous layer of cellulose and pectin, while germ pores are apertures in the exine where sporopollenin is absent.
Both intine and exine are composed exclusively of cellulose and lack any apertures.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Two-celled and three-celled pollen shedding stages

questiontext.text: In over 60 per cent of angiosperms, pollen grains are shed at the 2-celled stage. In the remaining species, how is the 3-celled stage formed before shedding?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A mature pollen grain contains a larger vegetative cell and a smaller generative cell.

Step 2: Application
In over 60 per cent of angiosperms, pollen grains are shed at this 2-celled stage. In the remaining species, the generative cell divides mitotically to give rise to two male gametes before the pollen grains are shed, resulting in a 3-celled stage (one vegetative cell and two male gametes).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The 3-celled stage is formed when the generative cell divides mitotically to produce two male gametes prior to shedding.

answer.text: The vegetative cell divides meiotically into two haploid cells.
The generative cell divides meiotically to form two male gametes.
The vegetative cell divides mitotically to form two male gametes.
The generative cell divides mitotically to give rise to two male gametes.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Parthenium as a cause of pollen allergy

questiontext.text: Which invasive plant species entered India as a contaminant with imported wheat and has become ubiquitous, causing severe pollen allergy and bronchial afflictions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pollen grains of many plant species can trigger severe allergies and chronic respiratory disorders such as asthma and bronchitis.

Step 2: Application
Parthenium (carrot grass), which came into India as a contaminant with imported wheat, has become ubiquitous in occurrence and is a major cause of pollen allergy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Parthenium (carrot grass) is the contaminant species responsible for widespread pollen allergies in India.

answer.text: Parthenium (carrot grass)
Vallisneria
Amorphophallus
Commelina

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - Pollen viability periods across plant families

questiontext.text: Pollen viability varies widely among angiosperms. Compare the viability period of pollen grains in cereals such as rice and wheat with that in members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae, and Solanaceae.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Once shed, pollen grains must land on a compatible stigma before losing viability; the duration of viability depends on the species as well as prevailing temperature and humidity.

Step 2: Application
In some cereals such as rice and wheat, pollen grains lose viability within 30 minutes of their release. In contrast, in some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae, and Solanaceae, pollen grains maintain viability for months.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pollen grains lose viability within 30 minutes in rice and wheat, whereas they remain viable for months in members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae, and Solanaceae.

answer.text: Months in rice and wheat; within 30 minutes in Rosaceae, Leguminosae, and Solanaceae
Within 30 minutes in rice and wheat; for months in Rosaceae, Leguminosae, and Solanaceae
Several years in rice and wheat; within 24 hours in Rosaceae, Leguminosae, and Solanaceae
Identical duration of about 48 hours across all four groups

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q11 - Cryopreservation of pollen grains in pollen banks

questiontext.text: For use in crop breeding programmes as pollen banks, pollen grains of a large number of species can be stored for years in which medium and at what temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Similar to seed banks, pollen banks preserve viable male gametophytes for long-term use in crop breeding programmes.

Step 2: Application
It is possible to store pollen grains of a large number of species for years in liquid nitrogen at \(-196^\circ\text{C}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pollen grains are cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen at \(-196^\circ\text{C}\) for pollen banks.

answer.text: 10% sugar solution at \(4^\circ\text{C}\)
Liquid carbon dioxide at \(-78^\circ\text{C}\)
Liquid nitrogen at \(-196^\circ\text{C}\)
Dry ice chambers at \(-20^\circ\text{C}\)

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q12 - Comparison of vegetative cell and generative cell

questiontext.text: Which of the following accurately distinguishes the vegetative cell from the generative cell in a mature 2-celled pollen grain?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Asymmetric mitotic division of a microspore produces two unequal cells in a mature pollen grain: a vegetative cell and a generative cell.

Step 2: Application
The vegetative cell is bigger, has abundant food reserves, and contains a large, irregularly shaped nucleus. The generative cell is small, spindle-shaped with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus, and floats in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The vegetative cell is larger with abundant food reserves and an irregularly shaped nucleus, whereas the generative cell is smaller, spindle-shaped, and floats in the vegetative cell's cytoplasm.

answer.text: The vegetative cell is spindle-shaped and floats in the cytoplasm of the larger generative cell.
The generative cell has abundant food reserves and a large irregularly shaped nucleus.
Both cells are equal in size and divide meiotically to form four male gametes.
The vegetative cell is larger with abundant food reserves and an irregularly shaped nucleus, while the generative cell is small, spindle-shaped, and floats in the vegetative cell's cytoplasm.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q13 - Parts of a pistil and location of placenta

questiontext.text: In a typical pistil, which part serves as the landing platform for pollen grains, and where is the placenta located?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each pistil consists of three parts: stigma, style, and ovary.

Step 2: Application
The stigma serves as the landing platform for pollen grains, the style is the elongated slender part beneath it, and the basal bulged part is the ovary. Inside the ovary is the ovarian cavity (locule), where the placenta is located and gives rise to ovules.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The stigma serves as the landing platform for pollen grains, and the placenta is located inside the ovarian cavity (locule).

answer.text: Stigma; inside the ovarian cavity (locule)
Style; on the outer wall of the thalamus
Stigma; inside the pollen sac
Ovary; at the tip of the style

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q14 - Syncarpous versus apocarpous gynoecium examples

questiontext.text: A multicarpellary gynoecium with fused pistils (syncarpous) and one with free pistils (apocarpous) are exemplified respectively by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When a gynoecium has more than one pistil (multicarpellary), the pistils may either be fused together (syncarpous) or remain free (apocarpous).

Step 2: Application
Papaver exhibits a multicarpellary, syncarpous pistil, whereas Michelia exhibits a multicarpellary, apocarpous gynoecium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Syncarpous and apocarpous multicarpellary gynoecia are exemplified by Papaver and Michelia, respectively.

answer.text: Michelia and Papaver
Papaver and Michelia
Hibiscus and wheat
Paddy and mango

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q15 - Ovule number per ovary across plant species

questiontext.text: Which group of plants is characterised by having only a single ovule in each ovary?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The number of ovules inside an ovary varies among angiosperms from one to many.

Step 2: Application
Wheat, paddy, and mango have a single ovule in each ovary, whereas papaya, water melon, and orchids contain many ovules in an ovary.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Wheat, paddy, and mango each possess a single ovule per ovary.

answer.text: Papaya, water melon, orchids
Papaya, wheat, orchids
Wheat, paddy, mango
Water melon, mango, orchids

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q16 - Structure of a typical angiosperm ovule

questiontext.text: In a typical angiosperm ovule, which region represents the junction between the body of the ovule and the funicle, and which part contains abundant reserve food materials enclosing the embryo sac?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An ovule (megasporangium) is attached to the placenta by a stalk called the funicle and is surrounded by protective integuments except at the micropyle.

Step 2: Application
The body of the ovule fuses with the funicle in the region called the hilum, which therefore represents the junction between the ovule and funicle. Enclosed within the integuments is a mass of cells called the nucellus, whose cells have abundant reserve food materials and enclose the embryo sac.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The hilum is the junction between the ovule and funicle, and the nucellus contains abundant reserve food materials enclosing the embryo sac.

answer.text: Chalaza and micropyle
Micropyle and integument
Chalaza and nucellus
Hilum and nucellus

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q17 - Megasporogenesis and megaspore mother cell

questiontext.text: Where does the megaspore mother cell (MMC) differentiate in a typical angiosperm ovule, and what is the immediate result of its meiotic division?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Megasporogenesis is the formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell (MMC).

Step 2: Application
Ovules generally differentiate a single large MMC (with dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus) in the micropylar region of the nucellus. The MMC undergoes meiotic division to produce four haploid megaspores.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The MMC differentiates in the micropylar region of the nucellus and undergoes meiosis to produce four megaspores.

answer.text: Micropylar region of the nucellus; four haploid megaspores
Chalazal region of the nucellus; two diploid megaspores
Funicle region; four diploid megaspores
Outer integument; one triploid megaspore

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q18 - Monosporic development of female gametophyte

questiontext.text: What is meant by monosporic development of the female gametophyte in a majority of flowering plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Meiosis of the megaspore mother cell yields four megaspores inside the ovule.

Step 2: Application
In a majority of flowering plants, only one of the four megaspores remains functional while the other three degenerate. Only this single functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac), which is termed monosporic development.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Monosporic development refers to the formation of the embryo sac from a single functional megaspore while the other three degenerate.

answer.text: All four megaspores fuse together to form a single embryo sac.
Only one functional megaspore develops into the embryo sac while the other three degenerate.
A single microspore develops directly into an ovule without meiosis.
Two functional megaspores jointly contribute nuclei to the central cell.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q19 - Free-nuclear mitotic divisions in embryo sac formation

questiontext.text: How many sequential free-nuclear mitotic divisions does the nucleus of the functional megaspore undergo to reach the 8-nucleate stage of the embryo sac?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During embryo sac development, nuclear divisions are strictly free-nuclear—meaning nuclear division is not immediately followed by cell wall formation—until the 8-nucleate stage is reached.

Step 2: Application
- First mitotic division: 1 nucleus divides into 2 nuclei (2-nucleate stage).
- Second mitotic division: 2 nuclei divide into 4 nuclei (4-nucleate stage).
- Third mitotic division: 4 nuclei divide into 8 nuclei (8-nucleate stage).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Three sequential free-nuclear mitotic divisions produce the 8-nucleate stage of the embryo sac.

answer.text: One meiotic and two mitotic divisions
Two sequential free-nuclear mitotic divisions
Three sequential free-nuclear mitotic divisions
Four sequential mitotic divisions with immediate cell wall formation

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q20 - Cellular organisation of 7-celled 8-nucleate embryo sac

questiontext.text: Why is a mature typical angiosperm embryo sac described as 7-celled yet 8-nucleate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
After the 8-nucleate stage, cell walls are laid down to organise the typical female gametophyte.

Step 2: Application
Six of the eight nuclei are surrounded by individual cell walls: three form the egg apparatus (two synergids and one egg cell) at the micropylar end, and three form the antipodals at the chalazal end. The remaining two nuclei (polar nuclei) lie together inside a single large central cell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because three cells are at the micropylar end, three at the chalazal end, and one large central cell houses two polar nuclei, the mature embryo sac has 7 cells and 8 nuclei.

answer.text: The egg cell is binucleate while the remaining six cells are uninucleate.
One of the antipodal cells contains two nuclei while the central cell is uninucleate.
Two synergids fuse into a single binucleate cell before fertilisation.
Six nuclei are enclosed in individual cells (3 in egg apparatus + 3 antipodals) while two polar nuclei share one large central cell.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q21 - Role and location of filiform apparatus

questiontext.text: Where is the filiform apparatus located in a mature embryo sac, and what is its specific role?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The egg apparatus at the micropylar end of the embryo sac consists of two synergids and one egg cell.

Step 2: Application
The synergids possess special cellular thickenings at their micropylar tip called the filiform apparatus, which plays an important role in guiding the pollen tubes into the synergid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The filiform apparatus is located at the micropylar tip of the synergids and guides the entry of the pollen tube into the synergid.

answer.text: At the micropylar tip of the synergids; guides the pollen tube into the synergid
At the chalazal end of the antipodals; nourishes the central cell
Around the polar nuclei; triggers triple fusion
In the outer integument; prevents entry of incompatible pollen

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q22 - Ploidy of nucellus, MMC, megaspore, and female gametophyte

questiontext.text: What is the correct sequence of ploidy levels for the cells of the nucellus, megaspore mother cell (MMC), functional megaspore, and female gametophyte, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sporophytic tissues of the ovule are diploid (\(2n\)), whereas meiotic products and the gametophyte derived from them are haploid (\(n\)).

Step 2: Application
1. Cells of the nucellus are sporophytic tissue, so they are diploid (\(2n\)).
2. The megaspore mother cell (MMC) differentiates from the nucellus prior to meiosis, so it is diploid (\(2n\)).
3. The functional megaspore is formed by meiosis of the MMC, so it is haploid (\(n\)).
4. The female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops by mitosis of the functional megaspore, so its cells are haploid (\(n\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The ploidy levels are \(2n, 2n, n, n\).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q23 - Xenogamy as source of genetically different pollen

questiontext.text: Which type of pollination is the only mechanism that brings genetically different types of pollen grains to the stigma during pollination?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Based on the source of pollen, pollination is divided into autogamy, geitonogamy, and xenogamy.

Step 2: Application
Autogamy involves transfer within the same flower, and geitonogamy involves transfer between different flowers of the same plant (hence genetically identical pollen). Only xenogamy transfers pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a different plant, bringing genetically different pollen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Xenogamy is the only type of pollination that brings genetically different pollen grains to the stigma.

answer.text: Autogamy
Geitonogamy
Xenogamy
Cleistogamy

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q24 - Cleistogamous flowers and assured seed-set

questiontext.text: Plants such as Viola, Oxalis, and Commelina produce cleistogamous flowers that do not open at all. What is a key reproductive feature of cleistogamous flowers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cleistogamous flowers remain closed, with anthers and stigma lying close to each other inside the bud.

Step 2: Application
Because these flowers never open, there is no chance of cross-pollen landing on the stigma. Thus, cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous and produce assured seed-set even in the absence of pollinators.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous and ensure seed-set even without pollinators.

answer.text: They require wind or insects to achieve cross-pollination.
They exhibit only xenogamy due to exposed anthers and stigma.
They cannot produce seeds unless pollinators visit them.
They are invariably autogamous and produce assured seed-set even in the absence of pollinators.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q25 - Functional vs genetic nature of geitonogamy

questiontext.text: Why is geitonogamy considered functionally similar to cross-pollination but genetically similar to autogamy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Geitonogamy is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of another flower on the same plant.

Step 2: Application
Because pollen moves from one flower to another, it involves a pollinating agent, making it functionally cross-pollination. However, since both flowers belong to the same individual plant, the pollen grains are genetically identical to those of the receiving flower, making it genetically similar to autogamy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Geitonogamy requires a pollinating agent (functionally cross-pollination) while transferring pollen from the same plant (genetically autogamy).

answer.text: It involves a pollinating agent between two flowers, but the pollen comes from the same plant.
It occurs inside a closed flower bud without any pollinating agent.
It transfers pollen between two different plants of the same species.
It involves fusion of two polar nuclei without male gametes.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q26 - Characteristics of wind-pollinated flowers

questiontext.text: Which combination of floral traits is characteristic of wind-pollinated (anemophilous) plants such as grasses?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Wind pollination requires adaptations that maximise pollen dispersal into air currents and capture of airborne pollen.

Step 2: Application
Wind-pollinated flowers produce light, non-sticky pollen grains in enormous numbers, possess well-exposed stamens, have large often-feathery stigmas, and typically contain a single ovule in each ovary with numerous flowers packed into an inflorescence (e.g., corn cob tassels). They are not very colourful and do not produce nectar.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Light, non-sticky pollen, well-exposed stamens, large feathery stigmas, and a single ovule per ovary are characteristic of wind-pollinated plants.

answer.text: Sticky pollen grains, colourful petals, nectar-rich flowers, many ovules per ovary
Light and non-sticky pollen, well-exposed stamens, large feathery stigma, single ovule per ovary
Foul-odoured flowers, ribbon-like pollen with mucilaginous covering
Unopened flowers with anthers and stigma enclosed inside the bud

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q27 - Water pollination in Vallisneria vs Zostera

questiontext.text: How does water pollination in Vallisneria differ from that in marine seagrasses such as Zostera?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pollination by water is limited to about 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons, and occurs either at the water surface or submerged inside water.

Step 2: Application
In Vallisneria (freshwater), the female flower reaches the surface of water by a long stalk and pollen grains are released onto the water surface, carried passively by water currents. In seagrasses like Zostera, female flowers remain submerged in water and long, ribbon-like pollen grains are released inside the water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In Vallisneria, pollination occurs on the water surface, whereas in Zostera, female flowers remain submerged and ribbon-like pollen grains are carried inside the water.

answer.text: Vallisneria is pollinated by insects while Zostera is pollinated by wind.
Vallisneria has submerged female flowers while Zostera raises female flowers above water.
In Vallisneria, female flowers reach the water surface and pollen floats on top; in Zostera, female flowers remain submerged and ribbon-like pollen is released inside water.
Both release spherical, dry pollen grains above the water surface.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q28 - Pollination in water hyacinth and water lily

questiontext.text: Although water hyacinth and water lily are aquatic plants, how are their flowers pollinated?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Not all aquatic plants use water as their pollinating agent.

Step 2: Application
In a majority of aquatic plants such as water hyacinth and water lily, the flowers emerge above the level of water and are pollinated by insects or wind, just like most land plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Flowers of water hyacinth and water lily emerge above the water level and are pollinated by insects or wind.

answer.text: By submerged water currents carrying ribbon-like pollen
Exclusively by cleistogamy underwater
By surface water currents carrying floating male flowers
By insects or wind, as their flowers emerge above the water level

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q29 - Mutualism between Yucca and moth and floral rewards

questiontext.text: In the mutualistic relationship between a species of moth and the plant Yucca, what floral reward does the plant provide to the moth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While nectar and pollen grains are the usual floral rewards for animal pollinators, some species provide safe places to lay eggs as a floral reward.

Step 2: Application
In Yucca (and similarly in Amorphophallus), the moth deposits its eggs in the locule of the ovary, and the flower gets pollinated by the moth in return. The moth larvae emerge from the eggs as the seeds start developing.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Yucca plant provides a safe place (the locule of the ovary) for the moth to lay its eggs.

answer.text: A safe place in the locule of the ovary to lay its eggs
Foul-smelling nectar secreted by the petals
Abundant dry, non-sticky pollen for adult feeding
Fleshy thalamus tissue for winter dormancy

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q30 - Definition of pollen and nectar robbers

questiontext.text: Floral visitors that consume pollen or nectar from a flower without bringing about pollination are referred to as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Only floral visitors that come into contact with both the anthers and the stigma can effect pollination.

Step 2: Application
Many insects consume pollen or nectar from flowers without contacting the anthers and stigma, and therefore do not bring about pollination; such visitors are called pollen/nectar robbers.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Visitors that consume floral rewards without effecting pollination are termed pollen/nectar robbers.

answer.text: Abiotic pollinators
Pollen/nectar robbers
Geitonogamous agents
Mutualistic pollinators

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q31 - Self-incompatibility as a genetic outbreeding device

questiontext.text: How does self-incompatibility prevent inbreeding in flowering plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Continued self-pollination leads to inbreeding depression, so plants have evolved outbreeding devices such as self-incompatibility.

Step 2: Application
Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that inhibits self-pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.

answer.text: By physically separating male and female flowers onto different plants
By keeping the flower petals permanently closed
By a genetic mechanism that inhibits self-pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil
By releasing pollen only after the ovules have degenerated

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q32 - Monoecious vs dioecious plants in preventing self-pollination

questiontext.text: Compare the effectiveness of monoecy (as in castor and maize) and dioecy (as in papaya) in preventing autogamy and geitonogamy.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Unisexual flowers can be borne on the same plant (monoecious) or on separate male and female plants (dioecious).

Step 2: Application
In monoecious plants like castor and maize, male and female flowers are separate on the same plant, which prevents autogamy (within the same flower) but cannot prevent geitonogamy (between different flowers of the same plant). In dioecious plants like papaya, each plant is exclusively male or female, which prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Monoecy prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy, whereas dioecy prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

answer.text: Monoecy prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy, while dioecy prevents only autogamy.
Both monoecy and dioecy prevent only autogamy and allow geitonogamy.
Monoecy prevents geitonogamy but not autogamy, while dioecy prevents only geitonogamy.
Monoecy prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy, whereas dioecy prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q33 - Pollen-pistil interaction and male gamete formation

questiontext.text: In angiosperms that shed pollen at the 2-celled stage, when and where does the generative cell divide to form the two male gametes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Following compatible pollination, the pollen grain germinates on the stigma to produce a pollen tube through a germ pore.

Step 2: Application
In plants where pollen is shed in the 2-celled condition (a vegetative cell and a generative cell), the generative cell divides mitotically to form the two male gametes during the growth of the pollen tube in the stigma.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The generative cell divides to form the two male gametes during the growth of the pollen tube in the stigma.

answer.text: During the growth of the pollen tube in the stigma
Inside the microsporangium prior to anther dehiscence
After the pollen tube enters the central cell
Inside the antipodal cells after double fertilisation

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q34 - Artificial hybridisation in unisexual female parents

questiontext.text: When performing artificial hybridisation on a female parent that produces unisexual flowers, which step is unnecessary?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Artificial hybridisation uses emasculation (removal of anthers from bisexual flower buds before dehiscence) and bagging to prevent unwanted pollen contamination.

Step 2: Application
If the female parent produces unisexual (pistillate) flowers, anthers are already absent, so there is no need for emasculation. However, bagging before the flowers open, dusting desired pollen when receptive, and rebagging are still required.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Emasculation is unnecessary when the female parent bears unisexual flowers.

answer.text: Bagging the female flower buds before they open
Emasculation using forceps
Dusting desired pollen onto the receptive stigma
Rebagging the pollinated flowers

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q35 - Syngamy and triple fusion in double fertilisation

questiontext.text: Double fertilisation in angiosperms consists of two fusion events inside the embryo sac. Which nuclei fuse during triple fusion, and what is the ploidy of the resulting primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
After entering a synergid, the pollen tube releases two haploid male gametes: one fuses with the egg cell (syngamy) to form the diploid zygote, and the other participates in triple fusion.

Step 2: Application
During triple fusion, one haploid male gamete (\(n\)) fuses with the two haploid polar nuclei (\(n + n\)) located in the central cell to produce a triploid (\(3n\)) primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
One male gamete fuses with two polar nuclei to form a triploid (\(3n\)) primary endosperm nucleus.

answer.text: One male gamete and the egg nucleus; diploid (\(2n\))
Two male gametes and one synergid nucleus; triploid (\(3n\))
One male gamete and two polar nuclei; triploid (\(3n\))
Three antipodal nuclei; triploid (\(3n\))

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q36 - Fate of central cell after triple fusion

questiontext.text: Immediately after triple fusion, what does the central cell become, and what structure does it develop into?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Double fertilisation produces two distinct structures: the zygote and the primary endosperm cell.

Step 2: Application
After triple fusion, the central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell (PEC) and develops into the endosperm, whereas the zygote develops into the embryo.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell (PEC) and develops into the endosperm.

answer.text: Zygote; develops into the embryo
Perisperm; develops into the seed coat
Nucellus; develops into the pericarp
Primary endosperm cell (PEC); develops into the endosperm

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q37 - Why endosperm development precedes embryo development

questiontext.text: In most angiosperms, the zygote remains dormant for some time and divides only after a certain amount of endosperm is formed. What is the adaptive significance of this?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Endosperm cells are filled with reserve food materials used for the nutrition of the developing embryo.

Step 2: Application
Endosperm development precedes embryo development as an adaptation to provide assured nutrition to the developing embryo once the zygote begins dividing.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Zygote division is delayed until endosperm forms so as to ensure assured nutrition for the developing embryo.

answer.text: It is an adaptation to provide assured nutrition to the developing embryo.
It allows the antipodals to divide and form the seed coat.
It prevents triple fusion from occurring in the central cell.
It induces parthenocarpy in the ovary wall.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q38 - Free-nuclear and cellular endosperm in tender coconut

questiontext.text: In a tender coconut, what do the liquid coconut water and the surrounding white kernel represent, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the most common type of endosperm development, the primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) undergoes successive free-nuclear divisions followed later by cell wall formation (cellularisation).

Step 2: Application
The coconut water from tender coconut is free-nuclear endosperm (made up of thousands of nuclei), and the surrounding white kernel is the cellular endosperm.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm, and the surrounding white kernel is cellular endosperm.

answer.text: Cellular endosperm and perisperm
Free-nuclear endosperm and cellular endosperm
Liquid nucellus and pericarp
Free-nuclear embryo and cotyledon

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q39 - Consumption vs persistence of endosperm in seeds

questiontext.text: In which of the following pairs of plants is the endosperm completely consumed by the developing embryo before seed maturation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Endosperm may either be completely consumed during embryo development or persist in the mature seed to be used during germination.

Step 2: Application
In pea, groundnut, and beans, the endosperm is completely consumed by the developing embryo before seed maturation (non-albuminous seeds). In contrast, endosperm persists in mature seeds of castor, coconut, wheat, and maize.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pea and groundnut have seeds in which the endosperm is completely consumed before seed maturation.

answer.text: Castor and coconut
Wheat and maize
Pea and groundnut
Barley and castor

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q40 - Dicot embryo axis, epicotyl, and hypocotyl

questiontext.text: In a typical dicotyledonous embryo, how are the epicotyl and hypocotyl defined relative to the level of attachment of the cotyledons?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical dicotyledonous embryo consists of an embryonal axis and two cotyledons.

Step 2: Application
The portion of the embryonal axis above the level of cotyledons is the epicotyl, which terminates with the plumule (stem tip). The cylindrical portion below the level of cotyledons is the hypocotyl, which terminates at its lower end in the radicle (root tip) covered with a root cap.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The epicotyl lies above the cotyledons and terminates in the plumule, while the hypocotyl lies below the cotyledons and terminates in the radicle.

answer.text: Epicotyl lies below the cotyledons terminating in the radicle; hypocotyl lies above terminating in the plumule.
Both epicotyl and hypocotyl lie above the cotyledons and terminate in the root cap.
Epicotyl forms the root cap; hypocotyl forms the two cotyledons.
Epicotyl lies above the cotyledons terminating in the plumule; hypocotyl lies below the cotyledons terminating in the radicle.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q41 - Structure of monocotyledonous grass embryo

questiontext.text: In the embryo of a grass (monocotyledon), what are the specific terms for the single lateral cotyledon and the hollow foliar structure enclosing the shoot apex?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Monocotyledonous embryos possess a single cotyledon and specialised protective sheaths around the shoot and root tips.

Step 2: Application
In the grass family, the single cotyledon situated laterally to the embryonal axis is called the scutellum. The epicotyl has a shoot apex and a few leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure called the coleoptile (while the radicle and root cap are enclosed in the coleorrhiza).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The single lateral cotyledon is the scutellum, and the hollow foliar structure enclosing the shoot apex is the coleoptile.

answer.text: Scutellum and coleoptile
Scutellum and coleorrhiza
Epiblast and coleorrhiza
Coleoptile and scutellum

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q42 - False fruits and contribution of thalamus

questiontext.text: Why are apple, strawberry, and cashew classified as false fruits?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Most fruits develop exclusively from the ovary and are called true fruits.

Step 2: Application
In a few species such as apple, strawberry, and cashew, the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation alongside the ovary; such fruits are called false fruits.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They are classified as false fruits because the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation.

answer.text: Because they develop without fertilisation and are seedless
Because the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation
Because their seeds contain persistent perisperm
Because they are formed from apomictic ovules

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q43 - Persistent nucellus as perisperm in seeds

questiontext.text: In seeds of black pepper and beet, what is the residual, persistent nucellus called?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While the nucellus is normally consumed during embryo sac and seed development, in a few species remnants of it persist in the mature seed.

Step 2: Application
In seeds such as black pepper and beet, the residual, persistent nucellus is termed perisperm (as distinct from pericarp, which is the fruit wall developed from the ovary wall).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The residual, persistent nucellus in black pepper and beet seeds is called the perisperm.

answer.text: Pericarp
Endosperm
Perisperm
Scutellum

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q44 - Seed micropyle, dehydration, and dormancy

questiontext.text: What is the functional significance of the small pore (micropyle) that remains in the hardened seed coat of a mature seed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As a seed matures, its integuments harden into tough protective seed coats, its moisture content drops to 10–15% by mass, and the embryo enters dormancy.

Step 2: Application
The micropyle remains as a small pore in the seed coat to facilitate the entry of oxygen and water into the seed during germination when favourable conditions return.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The micropyle in the seed coat facilitates the entry of oxygen and water into the seed during germination.

answer.text: It allows the pollen tube to exit the seed after germination.
It prevents moisture loss so the seed stays at 80% water content.
It serves as the attachment site of the pericarp to the thalamus.
It facilitates the entry of oxygen and water into the seed during germination.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q45 - Parthenocarpic fruits and hormone induction

questiontext.text: Fruits such as banana that develop without fertilisation are called parthenocarpic fruits. Which statement is true about parthenocarpy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Parthenocarpy is the formation of fruits without fertilisation.

Step 2: Application
Parthenocarpic fruits (such as banana) are seedless, and parthenocarpy can be induced artificially through the application of growth hormones.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Parthenocarpy can be induced through the application of growth hormones and yields seedless fruits.

answer.text: It can be induced through the application of growth hormones and produces seedless fruits.
It requires double fertilisation and always produces multiple seeds per fruit.
It is the formation of viable seeds without fertilisation in grasses.
It occurs only when the thalamus fuses with the pericarp.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q46 - Record seed viability in Lupinus arcticus and Phoenix dactylifera

questiontext.text: The oldest recorded viable seed (germinated after an estimated 10,000 years of dormancy) and a 2,000-year-old viable seed discovered near the Dead Sea belong, respectively, to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Seed viability after dispersal varies from a few months to hundreds or even thousands of years.

Step 2: Application
The oldest recorded viable seed is of a lupine, Lupinus arcticus, excavated from Arctic Tundra (germinated after ~10,000 years of dormancy). A 2,000-year-old viable seed is of the date palm, Phoenix dactylifera, discovered during archaeological excavation at King Herod's palace near the Dead Sea.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The 10,000-year-old and 2,000-year-old viable seeds belong to Lupinus arcticus and Phoenix dactylifera, respectively.

answer.text: Phoenix dactylifera and Lupinus arcticus
Lupinus arcticus and Phoenix dactylifera
Orobanche and Striga
Ficus and Lupinus arcticus

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q47 - Apomixis and its importance in hybrid seed industry

questiontext.text: Why is active research focused on transferring apomictic genes into hybrid crop varieties?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction by producing seeds without fertilisation (as seen in some Asteraceae and grasses).

Step 2: Application
Normally, if seeds collected from hybrid varieties are sown, the progeny segregate and lose hybrid characters, forcing farmers to buy costly hybrid seeds every year. If hybrids are made into apomicts, there is no segregation of characters in the progeny, so farmers can reuse hybrid seeds year after year.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Converting hybrids into apomicts prevents segregation of characters in the progeny, allowing farmers to reuse hybrid seeds across seasons without buying new seeds annually.

answer.text: Apomixis induces seedless parthenocarpic fruits in cereal crops.
Apomixis increases genetic segregation in every generation to create new varieties.
Apomixis prevents segregation of characters in hybrid progeny, allowing farmers to reuse hybrid seeds year after year.
Apomixis eliminates the need for endosperm nutrition during embryo development.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q48 - Polyembryony from nucellar cells in Citrus and Mango

questiontext.text: In many varieties of Citrus and Mango, polyembryony occurs when nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac divide, protrude into the embryo sac, and develop into embryos. What is the genetic nature of these nucellar embryos?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed. In Citrus and Mango, additional embryos arise from somatic nucellar cells.

Step 2: Application
Because nucellar cells are diploid (\(2n\)) sporophytic cells of the maternal parent and divide mitotically without meiosis or fertilisation, the resulting nucellar embryos are diploid and genetically identical to the parent plant (clones).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The nucellar embryos are diploid (\(2n\)) and genetically identical clones of the maternal parent.

answer.text: Haploid (\(n\)) and genetically diverse due to meiosis
Triploid (\(3n\)) and genetically identical to the endosperm
Diploid (\(2n\)) with new genetic combinations from syngamy
Diploid (\(2n\)) and genetically identical clones of the maternal parent
